flags.text: The bank explanation says the diagram shows "solid below the sublimation curve and gas above" and that 298 K and 1 atm is "above the sublimation curve". On the standard diagram (pressure up, temperature right) that is reversed: gas lies below and to the right of the boundary lines, and at 298 K the line that matters is the liquid-gas line, about 64 atm there. Bank text untouched; the explainer and picture put the point in the gas region, under the curves. Key unchanged.

The stem says the point falls "well below the triple-point pressure but above its temperature", which nearly reads the diagram for the student. Suggested wording for Thomas to review (not applied): drop that clause. Key unchanged.

served.stem: On the CO2 phase diagram, the triple point lies at 5.11 atm and 216.6 K, while the critical point is at 73 atm and 304 K. A sample of CO2 is held at 1.00 atm and 25°C (298 K), conditions that fall well below the triple-point pressure but above its temperature. What phase is the CO2 in?
served.bankWhy: At 1 atm (below 5.11 atm triple-point pressure) liquid CO2 is unstable, so the diagram shows only solid below the sublimation curve and gas above. At 298 K and 1 atm we are above the sublimation curve, so CO2 exists as a gas.

answer.line: 1 atm is under CO2's triple-point pressure, 5.11 atm, and below that pressure liquid cannot exist. At 298 K it is gas.

steps: Locate the point: 1 atm and 298 K. Compare the pressure with the triple point first: 1 atm is well under 5.11 atm.
Know what that means. Below the triple-point pressure only solid and gas exist; liquid CO2 needs more than 5.11 atm.
Check the temperature: 298 K is far above 195 K, where dry ice sublimes at 1 atm. So the point is gas.

choices.note: Supercritical CO2 needs T above 304 K and P above 73 atm. 1 atm is nowhere near.
Solid and liquid coexist only on the melting line, which starts at the triple point, 5.11 atm. This point sits far below it.
At 1 atm CO2 is solid only below about 195 K, as dry ice. At 298 K it has long since sublimed.
Under the curves at 298 K and 1 atm: gas.
Water is liquid at room conditions, so liquid feels natural. CO2 is the exception: its liquid needs more than 5.11 atm.

student.lockIt: Below the triple-point pressure there is no liquid: the substance goes straight between solid and gas.
